lines.text: You'll be off up the Reach, then. I drove cattle up there. We didn't go out of this gate, we went out of the old gate down past the mill, and they'd no cause to move it that I ever saw. Grass does well up on the Reach. Which is — anyway. Mind the gate on your way through.
Skir come over the hedge at dusk, hunting the Nibbin out of the tussock. I've watched one drop and come up with nothing at all, and go up again, and drop again twenty foot along.
I had cattle on the Reach fifty-two years. Or fifty. My daughter has it wrote down somewhere. I've told you about the gate already, I should think.
The Reach has come up green right down to the fence line this year. The grass didn't come that far down the slope when I was droving.

Tolm will get a crop off his west side out of a year like this one. His father had that field in oats and the oats did all right down there. Then Tolm put it down to grass when he took it on. He'll have had a reason.
The Reach is short this year. I'd have had the beasts down off that rise a month early.

The town fields go the way the Reach goes. Tolm's west side goes first, and it went first the year of the wet harvest as well. He tells me it's his drainage doing it. I didn't follow the half of what he did down there.
Maren let me hold the survey book. It's numbers all down the page and not one drawing.
There's a Nibbin lives under the mill step and I gave her a name. I said her name to Maren and she wrote down one Nibbin. Da says I'm not to keep on at her. I'm going to keep on at her about it.
When I'm bigger I'm walking all the way up to the Sanctum Fallow on my own. It's shut, but there's a wall down at the back of it. I'm going up to look at the wall.
The lanterns were better when I was small. They say it's the same lanterns and it's me that got bigger. They were bigger, though. I remember.
The Nibbin under the mill step has gone white round the face. She's the same one, I'd know her anywhere. Maren wrote her down again and the book still just says Nibbin.
West gate's down again. Bramblehog, same post as last time. Back up before dark.
Loamunder in the furrows all night. Stand in the west field after dark and you can hear them under the ground. I've ploughed it top and bottom and never turned one up.
Six weeks to harvest. Two hands, four fields. Tolm's taking another pair on once the crop's in, which is a bit after I want them.

A track's the easy sign. A browse line takes longer. That's where something's come along and eaten the tips off a bush and left the stems standing. Which is to say the bush is still stood there. With me?

Pollywisp you only get in the spring. Every summer somebody stops me to say the Pollywisp have gone out of the Reach. They're down in the wet ground, which is to say you won't see them till the spring.
I measure the browse height off a folding rule. Cut the notches on it myself.
Fence line's four miles. I walk it spring and back end and mend what's down. Cart gets to the second stile. I carry the rest.
Something comes through the wire down the west end. Takes the post clean out of the ground with it. It's heavy, whatever it is. Post's in the barrow if you want a look at it.
Warden wants a number off me. I showed her the post. She wrote something down.
This is the third year I've come up for the picking. The grass is further on than it was this same week last year. Four or five days further on, I'd say.
The tussock's crept north on me as well. Where I was picking last year is bare ground now, and I make it a hundred paces from the old edge to the new one. Wet springs, I'd say.
There's a stone up on the north rise cut into a pair of antlers. No idea what it's for.
I walked the whole tussock this morning and turned up two Nibbin. Two. Last year I'd have seen a dozen before I got as far as the gate.
The Skir are still about, only they're over the far hedge now instead of the rise. I'm up here three weeks a year, so there's a good deal I don't see.
I've not picked the Reach this thick before. The grass is knee-high on the north rise and the same week last year it was no higher than my boot.
The Nibbin have been grazing that rise all week and there's still grass standing. I put a Bramblehog up on the path this morning and it barely got out of my way.
Lanterns are up on the green. They go up the last week of the season, and when the season's out the year goes over with it.

Every beast on the place gets a year older at the turn. Makes no odds whether it's been out on the grass all year or shut up in the byre since spring. We'd bring the beasts down off the Reach the week before, most years.
Same four miles I had six years ago. Still one man on it.
I put the posts back in the same holes I dug six years ago. Three down the west end won't hold now without stone packed round. So I carry stone up with me.
The tussock's gone six hundred paces north of where I picked my first year up here. Six years of that. I pace it out the same week every year.

The tracker out of Hearthollow says it's the water under the ground, shifting with whatever's been grazed off up top. I still say it's the wet springs. She's here the year round and I'm here three weeks of it.
